title: Columnstore for a Telemetry Roll-Up
description: A per-sensor roll-up over millions of rows scans the rowstore in row mode; a nonclustered columnstore index aggregates it in batch mode. Why it matters: telemetry and IoT-style data (huge row counts, simple aggregates) is an increasingly common workload shape, and columnstore is the standard modern answer for it.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Telemetry and IoT-style data has a very distinctive shape compared to typical business data: an enormous number of rows (a fleet of sensors each reporting readings every few seconds adds up to millions of rows astonishingly fast), but each row is narrow and simple — usually just a sensor ID, a timestamp, and a reading or two. And the questions people actually ask of this data are almost always aggregate questions across huge swaths of it: 'what's the average reading per sensor,' 'what's the max temperature per device over the last day,' 'how many readings came in per hour.' Nobody typically needs to fetch one single telemetry row by itself — the value is almost always in summarizing across thousands or millions of them at once. This combination — huge volume, narrow rows, aggregate-heavy queries — is becoming an increasingly standard workload shape as more systems collect continuous sensor, log, or event data, and it's worth recognizing as its own category with its own standard solution.

A normal SQL Server table, stored as a rowstore (organized row by row, with every column of a row physically stored together on the same page), is a poor match for this shape, even though it's the default and the obvious choice when you first create the table. To compute an average reading per sensor across 800,000 rows, the engine has to pull every single full row through its processing pipeline — reading the sensor ID, the timestamp, the reading value, and any other columns on that row, one row at a time, in what's called **row-mode execution**. Even though the aggregate query only actually cares about two of those columns, rowstore forces you to drag the whole row past the CPU to get at them, because that's simply how the data is laid out on disk — column values you don't need are sitting right next to the ones you do, packed together on the same pages.

This is exactly the kind of workload where a **nonclustered columnstore index** earns its keep. Instead of storing data row-by-row, a columnstore index reorganizes the specific columns it covers into a column-by-column layout: every `SensorId` value packed together, every `Reading` value packed together, each compressed heavily (telemetry data is often very compressible — a sensor's readings tend to cluster in a narrow range, and there are usually far fewer distinct sensor IDs than there are total readings, both of which compress well). On top of the compression, columnstore unlocks **batch-mode execution** — instead of the engine processing telemetry rows one at a time, it processes them in batches of roughly 900 rows at once, using CPU instructions that operate on many values simultaneously rather than one-by-one, similar in spirit to how specialized signal-processing hardware crunches many samples per instruction rather than one sample at a time. For a workload that's fundamentally 'aggregate a huge number of simple numeric readings,' this combination of columnar storage, heavy compression, and batch processing is close to a best-case scenario — it's specifically engineered for exactly this kind of bulk numeric summarization.

An important detail carried over from earlier lessons on this same topic: a *nonclustered* columnstore index sits alongside the table's existing rowstore structure rather than replacing it. This matters for telemetry systems specifically because many of them still need occasional point-style operations too — inserting new readings as they arrive, or looking up a specific device's most recent reading for a live status check. Those operations keep using the normal rowstore path exactly as before, completely unaffected, while the heavy aggregate/reporting queries automatically get routed by the optimizer to the columnstore copy instead. This dual-path capability — fast inserts and point lookups on one side, fast bulk analytics on the other, both against the very same live table — is the **HTAP** (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing) pattern, and it's specifically why nonclustered columnstore has become close to a default recommendation for telemetry and IoT-style tables in modern SQL Server designs: you get a data warehouse's aggregation speed without needing a separate warehouse or an ETL pipeline copying data somewhere else on a delay.

What to look for in a plan showing this problem: a **Clustered Index Scan** reading the full rowstore table, feeding into a row-mode Hash Match or Stream Aggregate, for a query whose shape is fundamentally 'aggregate across a huge number of rows using only a couple of narrow columns' — exactly the telemetry pattern. The fix is to add a nonclustered columnstore index covering the columns the aggregate queries actually use (here, `SensorId` and `Reading`), letting the optimizer automatically prefer the compressed, batch-mode columnstore path for these heavy rollups while the table's ordinary write and point-lookup traffic continues completely unaffected on the original rowstore structure.

## Scenario
An analytics query averages readings per sensor over 800,000 telemetry rows. On the rowstore clustered index it reads the entire table, row by row, every time.

## Why it's slow
The clustered index is **row-oriented**: to average one column it still pulls whole rows through the engine, one at a time (row mode). For a scan-everything aggregation, that's a lot of wasted I/O and CPU — rowstore is built for point lookups and small ranges, not for crunching a whole column.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** feeding a hash aggregate, touching the full table in row mode.
- An analytical query (`SUM`/`AVG`/`COUNT ... GROUP BY`) over a large table.

## The concept
Add a **nonclustered columnstore index** on the aggregated columns. Columnstore stores data by column in compressed segments and processes it in **batch mode** (hundreds of rows per CPU step), so a per-sensor average scans far less data far faster. Nonclustered columnstore lets the same table keep serving OLTP lookups on the rowstore while analytics use the columnstore — the HTAP pattern.
hints: The rowstore clustered index is scanned in row mode to aggregate a whole column -- the wrong storage for analytics.
A columnstore index stores data by column and processes it in batch mode, ideal for SUM/AVG/COUNT over big tables.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Measurements ON Measurements(SensorId, Reading); then re-run.
